Expectation1: Provide guidance and wisdom based on life experience
Situation1: A grandchild brings up a general question about navigating a new phase of their life.
Situation2: Your friend has misunderstood the tone of your text message and replied sounding hurt. You need to call them right now to explain.
Story: I was sitting at the kitchen table, sipping tea, when my granddaughter plopped down across from me, her eyes full of questions. “Grandma, how did you know what to do when you started your first job?” she asked, her voice uncertain. I could see she needed reassurance, maybe a story from my own life to help her feel less alone in her worries. Just as I opened my mouth to answer, my phone buzzed. It was a message from my friend, Linda. Her reply was curt, her words clipped—she’d clearly misunderstood my earlier text, and I could feel the sting in her tone. I knew I should call her right away, clear things up before the hurt deepened. But my granddaughter was waiting, looking to me for wisdom and comfort. My heart tugged in two directions: the urge to be the steady, wise grandparent she needed, and the responsibility to be a good friend, to communicate openly and mend the rift. I sat there, torn, the weight of both roles pressing on me, unsure which need to answer first.
